stem: A client has significant bilateral lower-extremity weakness and needs an assistive device for ambulation. Which device generally provides the most appropriate base of support among these options?

options.A: A single-point cane, because it provides enough support for bilateral leg weakness while preserving the smallest possible base of support.
options.B: A quad cane, because it is generally preferred over walkers when both lower extremities are weak and substantial stability is required.
options.C: A standard walker, because its broad support base is appropriate when bilateral leg weakness creates a need for improved gait stability.
options.D: No assistive device, because walking without external support promotes recovery more safely than using a walker in bilateral leg weakness.

rationale: MedlinePlus states that a cane is appropriate when only a little help with balance or stability is needed and advises that crutches or a walker may be better when there is substantial weakness or balance difficulty. Given significant bilateral lower-extremity weakness and the listed choices, a standard walker provides the most appropriate broader support. The cane choices provide less support, and no device does not address the stated stability need.
educational_objective: Select a walker rather than a cane when substantial bilateral lower-extremity weakness creates a greater need for external gait support.
source_locator: Introductory guidance: cane is a good choice for a little help with balance/stability or mild weakness; with a lot of weakness or balance problems, crutches or a walker may be better.
source_claim_supported: MedlinePlus distinguishes cane use for limited support from walker/crutch use when weakness or balance problems are substantial.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — mobility, positioning, and assistive care.

source_original.stem: A client has significant bilateral lower-extremity weakness and needs an assistive device for ambulation. Which device generally provides the most appropriate base of support among these options?

options.A: A single-point cane, because it provides enough support for bilateral leg weakness while preserving the smallest possible base of support.
options.B: A quad cane, because it is generally preferred over walkers when both lower extremities are weak and substantial stability is required.
options.C: A standard walker, because its broad support base is appropriate when bilateral leg weakness creates a need for improved gait stability.
options.D: No assistive device, because walking without external support promotes recovery more safely than using a walker in bilateral leg weakness.

source_original.rationale: Merck notes that walkers provide greater stability than canes and are particularly appropriate when bilateral leg weakness contributes to fall risk. Option C is correct because a standard walker provides a broad base of support. Option A offers less support with a single-point cane. Option B offers a larger cane base but still less overall support than a walker for substantial bilateral weakness. Option D removes external support despite the stated mobility deficit.
source_original.source_detail: Using a Cane: a cane is appropriate when only a little help with balance/stability or one-sided weakness is needed; with substantial weakness or balance problems, crutches or a walker may be more appropriate. Among the listed options, a walker provides the broadest support for bilateral weakness. MedlinePlus patient instruction reviewed 2025-04-01; current NLM resource rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Basic Care and Comfort: mobility, positioning, skin integrity, elimination and nonpharmacologic comfort activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Corrected the rationale's source attribution from Merck to the actual cited MedlinePlus source and avoided claiming a universal device rule beyond the substantial-weakness context presented in the stem.

audit_findings.exact_locator: Opening cane-selection guidance directly contrasts limited cane support with walker/crutch support for substantial weakness/balance problems.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Removed unsupported Merck attribution and did not claim walkers are always required for bilateral weakness.

distractor_audit.B: Still provides less support than a walker for the stated need.
distractor_audit.C: Best matches MedlinePlus guidance among listed options.
distractor_audit.D: Fails to provide needed external support.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: C is uniquely best given significant bilateral weakness and the available choices.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are device-selection statements tied to support needs.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits Basic Care and Comfort mobility support.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Second pass focused on whether the source actually establishes walker superiority; final wording limits the claim to substantial weakness and the listed options.
